items.summary: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. We predicted our final score to four decimal places prior to submission. We report negative results at equal length, and give a full account of data provenance and compliance in Section 8, including a full account of every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.

The isolated Kalman filter (IsoKF) of Jung, Luft and Weiss (Autonomous Robots, 2025) lets the nodes of a robot or sensor network share an estimation task cheaply: only the nodes involved in a measurement update, and their correlations with everyone else are rescaled by a correction factor. Its authors conjectured that for any completely observable and controllable system the covariance it reports converges to a finite, unique, stable steady state. Result: the conjecture is false. A three-node system with pair-sum observations x1+x2, x2+x3, x3+x1 and dynamics A = 3I is observable from one epoch and controllable, every local block the filter uses stays positive definite, yet the reported marginal variances satisfy m_k ≥ (5/4)(9/5)^k − 1/4, while the centralised Kalman filter keeps every variance at most 3/4. A Perron-root comparison extends divergence to every connected non-bipartite pair-sum graph when a^2 is large enough; extra attenuation or deletion of cross-covariances does not help. Schur-stable dynamics always give bounded marginals (proved). Computer-assisted proofs (outward-rounded interval arithmetic) show that for a^2 in (1, 1.38] large priors diverge at rate a^(2k), entry certified from 10^12 I at eight values down to a^2 = 1 + 10^-8, and that at a^2 = 21/20 the prior I converges while 10^12 I diverges: there is no globally attracting steady covariance. Also: exact classification of participant overlaps (|U ∩ V| ≤ 1) that keep every local block positive definite, and a bounded regime for anchored relative measurements. Scope: in high-precision numerical tests the actual estimation error stays bounded; the failure is gross pessimism of the reported covariance, not divergence of the estimate. The counterexample uses pair-sum measurements, not plain differences. Nothing is proved for a^2 in (1.38, 2+√5); uniqueness for stable dynamics remains open. The ikf_lib software was inspected but not run; no software failure is claimed. Version 0.2.0 (correction). Version 0.1.0 compared this work with Luft, Schubert, Roumeliotis and Burgard (2018, IJRR, doi:10.1177/0278364918760698) at abstract level only. This version compares it with the full text: Luft et al. introduce the correction factor (their eq. 26) and a scaled variant (eq. 28), and prove that two-robot blocks stay positive definite (Proposition 1, now credited at Theorem 8.1 and Corollary 5.3); they make no claim about boundedness or convergence of the covariance and give no divergence example. The two citing works are now also compared in full text. No theorem, proof, certificate, computation or numerical finding changed. items.summary: Scientific agents can find interventions that work without understanding why they do. We study this failure mode in controlled synthetic regulatory systems, where agents must experimentally identify a hidden fault and rescue the resulting phenotype. Across seven LLMs, every model restores the healthy phenotypes more often than it identifies the fault. Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 rescue every organism while diagnosing only 55% and 35% of them. This failure is not simply due to insufficient exploration or unavailable evidence. In most cases, the cause is experimentally identifiable, and agents encounter evidence that distinguishes competing causes in 91% of relevant sessions, and still frequently misdiagnose the system. Targeted probes reveal where experimental reasoning breaks down. Models reliably interpret decisive evidence and revise hypotheses when the causal comparison is explicit, and can locate that evidence within a full experimental record. However, they struggle to predict the outcome of the experiment under each competing cause, a necessary step in using the observed result to distinguish between them. Agents can therefore gather the right evidence and still infer the wrong cause. As AI systems take on a growing role in synthesising scientific evidence, these findings highlight the need to evaluate how they use evidence to reach causal conclusions, alongside whether their interventions succeed.
items.title: Treating the Symptom, Missing the Cause: Anatomy of a Scientific Reasoning Failure

Version of record: SSRN 7390698 , DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7390698 . Cite that version. The same text is also at https://polyhelper.ai/research/agreement-not-evidence/ and https://github.com/vadimchernets/papers/tree/main/agreement-not-evidence . Someone who asks one language model a question cannot tell a confidently wrong answer from a confidently right one. The two are identical on every surface cue available to a non-expert. Asking several models seems to solve this, but it mostly relocates the problem: reconciling several answers produces one confident text again, and that text now carries the borrowed authority of "ten of them agreed." The protocol formalized here collects answers from several consumer chat models through the user's own browser or phone, with no API keys, no installation and no intermediary server. It reconciles them by anchor-and-enrich: the strongest available answer becomes the base, and each of the others contributes only what the base lacks. Every contribution is signed with the model that supplied it. Disagreements are kept in a section of their own rather than averaged away. The paper makes four contributions. The first is the protocol itself, stated as an algorithm that preserves provenance and forbids silent deletion, together with a taxonomy of five ways a merge can fail. Four of them are defects of naive pooling; the fifth is a failure of the operator rather than of the method: a synthesis that presents a single model's output as a collegial result. The second is the application of the correlated-witness arithmetic to protocol design. That arithmetic is not claimed here. Kohli (2026) applied the same Kish correction to a panel of nine frontier judges and measured about two effective votes, and Kim et al. (2025) established the underlying error correlation across more than 350 models. A council of N models whose errors carry intraclass correlation ρ is worth = N / (1 + (N−1)ρ) independent witnesses, and that quantity saturates at 1/ρ however many models are added. Once a council is larger than 1/ρ, halving ρ beats doubling N, and a pair with low error correlation can outweigh five with high correlation. Which pairs those are is measured, not read off the label: the larger and more accurate models carry the most correlated errors even when architecture and provider differ (Kim et al., 2025), and the author's per-pair measurements found no detectable effect of geopolitical bloc on error correlation and, in the pairs measured, none of shared lineage (Chernets, 2026). Conditioning the second model raises ρ in exchange for error correction. items.summary: Wave energy converters (WECs) are typically designed to operate near resonance to maximize energy capture. While this enhances power absorption, it also amplifies structural loads and accelerates fatigue damage. As a result, fatigue becomes a critical design driver even when stress remains below material yield limits. Fatigue in offshore systems has been widely studied, particularly under variable-amplitude loading induced by waves, wind, and currents. These effects are commonly evaluated using the Palmgren–Miner damage accumulation rule, where failure is predicted once cumulative damage reaches unity. However, fatigue assessment for WECs remains less developed, especially in terms of linking environmental conditions to structural degradation and operational stress limits. The objective of this work is to evaluate, predict and improve confidence in the structural response and fatigue life of a WEC under representative operating conditions and to identify critical components and failure modes before deployment in March 2026 accounting for not only load and geometric factors, but also environmental conditions such as temperature.

items.summary: We investigate the automated generation of executable robot reinforcement learning (RL) policies from natural-language task descriptions. Rather than using large language models (LLMs) as execution-time decision makers, we use them as designers that construct RL pipelines before deployment, including Markov decision process (MDP) formulation and simulator implementation. We identify a phase-wise structure in this problem: MDP formulation is dependency-structured and sequential, whereas simulator implementation becomes modular once the formulation is fixed. Based on this structure, we propose ARPG, a dependency-aware agentic framework that performs sequential MDP modeling, localized verification and correction, and simulator-structured implementation while externalizing intermediate artifacts. ARPG targets a key failure mode of automated policy generation: executable code may still yield non-learnable policies when state, action, reward, and termination artifacts are not semantically aligned. Experiments in Isaac Sim show that ARPG improves modeling correctness, environment executability, and policy-generation success compared with monolithic LLM baselines and off-the-shelf agentic systems. Additional demonstrations on custom robotics, standard RL, and engineering-domain MDPs further suggest that the same modeling pipeline can be reused beyond the main benchmark suite.

items.summary: Real-world geospatial decision support requires more than single-step retrieval or code generation. Disaster-response questions often involve multi-source workflows that combine spatial databases, map-derived features, satellite imagery, raster products, and reusable geospatial artifacts, where correctness depends on preserving spatial scope, temporal context, and intermediate execution state. While large language models and coding agents offer a promising interface for such workflows, they struggle with geospatial-specific failure modes, including handling large artifacts, selecting the wrong evidence source, losing spatial or temporal metadata, and applying invalid geometric operations. We introduce GeoFaham, a domain-specialized multi-agent system for geospatial disaster analytics. GeoFaham decomposes workflows into specialist agents for vector operations, map feature retrieval, imagery discovery, and raster analysis, coordinated by an Orchestrator with a dual-ledger control loop for dependency-aware planning, progress tracking, validation, and replanning. To support artifact-centric collaboration, GeoFaham uses a Response Store that persists full geospatial outputs and typed metadata outside the LLM context window while agents exchange compact identifiers and summaries. We also introduce GeoFaham-Bench, a 40-task benchmark grounded in 17 real-world disaster records, designed to evaluate multi-step geospatial reasoning, cross-source integration, raster-vector computation, artifact generation, and recovery under non-rigid ground truth. We evaluate GeoFaham on GeoFaham-Bench against strong general-purpose coding-agent baselines, including Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode. GeoFaham achieves the best overall performance, scoring 0.940 versus the next-best 0.879, while using 7.5 times fewer tokens. Our code and benchmark are publicly available at https://github.com/microsoft/GeoFaham.
items.title: GeoFaham: Domain-Specialized Multi-Agent Geospatial Analytics for Disaster Response

items.summary: On a public agent leaderboard, a general-purpose agent trails a scaffold built for an airline customer-service benchmark by 13 points on the tasks that touch its database, and a reader could conclude that generality costs accuracy. The gap comes from the grader. The general agent often ends its conversations in a way that never triggers grading, so only about half of its episodes were scored and the rest were stored as failures. Grading the ungraded half under the benchmark's own rule closes the pooled gap, without rerunning any agent. We audit two carefully maintained public leaderboards, HAL and tau2-bench, from their published artifacts alone and find three more instrument errors. A cost column counts nested model calls twice, unevenly across rows. Archived trajectories record grader-written actions as agent actions. Re-grading saved trajectories under a newer evaluator is itself a new measurement: a correct and announced fix reorders a leaderboard, and a mode check that misreads four files collapses their scores by 59 to 82 points while printing no error. Each produced a plausible number, and the HAL maintainers confirmed their three within five weeks. Together the cases show that the infrastructure of agent evaluation, meaning the code that grades, logs, replays and versions an evaluation, is part of the measurement and fails silently, so scores and orderings can move with no visible sign. These failure modes follow from how agent evaluation pipelines are built, and those pipelines change as fast as the agents they measure, so we expect more of them elsewhere. We propose cheap checks that expose the instrument: report the graded fraction, aggregate cost from root spans, tag the provenance of every recorded action, and pin evaluator versions with a published re-grade diff.
items.title: Silent Instrument Errors Reorder Agent Leaderboards

items.summary: Split Inference (SI) addresses the hardware resource limitations of Internet of Things (IoT) devices by distributing tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) model segments across multiple IoT devices. However, a device failure can interrupt the inference pipeline. This paper proposes a replica-aware recovery approach that deploys replicas of TinyML model segments originally hosted on failed devices onto surviving devices. We formulate the joint selection of replica hosts and communication protocols as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem that minimizes post-reconfiguration inference latency, accounting for computation and transmission latencies, under flash memory and runtime memory constraints. Simulations using MobileNetV2 on heterogeneous IoT networks compare the proposed approach with four baselines. We implement the model in a network of 15 IoT devices with a maximum link-rate reduction of 75%, and show that MILP approach achieves an average modeled end-to-end inference latency that is 6.8% lower than that of Computation Greedy and 18.3% lower than that of Random. Index Terms TinyML, split inference, Internet of Things, fault tolerance, replica placement.
items.title: Replica-Aware Split Inference for Edge IoT Systems

items.summary: Science is a process of useful models being proven wrong time and again, but despite its many flaws, it somehow works. Why is this? Paul Feyerabend argued that it works because people dare to hold and defend incompatible rival theories against the accepted one, since a theory's failures often lead to its abandonment in the presence of a more accurate or simpler alternative. He called this view theoretical pluralism. We introduce a theoretical and experimental model in which this can be examined. It compares communities of pluralist agents, which can hold rival theories side by side and maintain beliefs within and between those theories, with communities of monist agents, which can only incorporate what they hear or observe into a single model of their own. In a multi-agent variational inference setting, our experimental demonstrations illustrate how communities with rival theories can go through periods of uncertainty followed by a shift in the theories they hold true, how the information that is communicated between communities affects beliefs when those communities make different observations about the world, and how sharing support for theories and sharing beliefs within them contribute differently to collective belief dynamics.

items.summary: Large foundation models often answer even when the available visual or textual evidence is insufficient to support a reliable conclusion. This failure to abstain makes them hard to trust in high-stakes or information-seeking settings, where a confident but unsupported answer can be worse than no answer at all. We present Dr. No, a feature-steering approach that mines sparse autoencoder (SAE) features associated with abstention and commitment, then modulates a small set of them during the prefill pass, without retraining the base model. Dr. No is evaluated on LLaVA-1.6 Mistral 7B across multimodal abstention benchmarks, including UNK-VQA and MM-UPD, and additionally benchmarked on language reasoning tasks using Qwen3.5-2B on AbstentionBench subsets. Against multiple uncertainty-based abstention baselines, feature steering achieves a more favourable balance between correct answering and appropriate abstention than post-hoc rejection methods. items.summary: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.

items.summary: LLM agents struggle to automate complex enterprise procedures because static, pre-built harness cannot capture proprietary policies, undocumented behaviors, or state-dependent recovery paths that surface only during execution. Procedural memory accrued from agent experience offers a training-free path to closing this gap -- yet unlike episodic records or semantic facts, it must consolidate repeated successes and diagnosed failures into reusable actions and recovery strategies. Our results reveal that prescriptive knowledge organization such as human defined schemas and explicit deduplication rules hurts performance rather than closing the procedural-knowledge gap. In contrast, human diagnosis converts failed traces into corrective knowledge and drives sustained improvement: a single round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0-10.9%. These findings point to a simple division of labor: let agents organize procedural memory, and invest human effort where it matters most -- diagnosis.

Low-dimensional interventions further separate source-role information from answer-value information. Their effects peak at different depths, and changing the source-role signal does not eliminate the causal influence of competing values. These findings support a failure of downstream evidence use beyond source identification alone: source-role information can influence a decision without exclusively controlling which historical values affect it. Reliable conversational memory therefore requires not only retention and retrieval, but also control over how retained information enters answer computation.

items.summary: Abstract: Keeping the modern power grid running during heatwaves, wildfires, or cyberattacks requires knowing which power lines are the most dangerous "dominoes" if two or three of them fail at the same time. However, checking every possible combination of multiple broken lines across the Western U.S. grid is a math problem with millions of possibilities—far too slow for computers to solve in real time using standard physics equations. Conversely, taking shortcuts by simply looking at a map of the grid (to find the biggest, most connected hubs) fails because electricity does not travel like cars on a highway; it cannot be told which road to take. Instead, electricity automatically splits across all available wires based on their physical resistance. When a major line gets crowded or breaks, electricity surges onto smaller side-lines, causing chain-reaction blackouts far away from the original problem. In this memo, we introduce Physics-Informed Network Reshaping (PINR), an AI framework that bridges the gap between map-based speed and physical accuracy. PINR combines a specialized, mathematically predictable neural network with a network-disruption algorithm originally designed for counter-terrorism. Rather than testing millions of broken-wire combinations one by one, PINR uses a single, rapid pass to act as a dual-use stress gauge: For Grid Defenders ("Blue Team" Healing): It shows grid operators the exact 27 congested power lines where slightly "throttling" the flow (like adjusting valves on a water pipe) relieves 99.1% of grid overloads during a peak evening crunch, pushing excess electricity safely onto underused backup lines. For Security Analysts ("Red Team" Vulnerability Hunting): Because the lines that need the most throttling to heal the grid are the exact same lines carrying the most dangerous physical stress, PINR automatically narrows the search for catastrophic multi-line failures from 235 lines down to just 27. This cuts the number of three-line failure combinations to check by 99.86% (from over 2.1 million down to under 3,000). Most importantly, testing PINR on the 2026 Western Energy Imbalance Market (WEIM) proves that looking at a static map of the grid is dangerously misleading. While standard map-based analysis points to California's central grid hub (CAISO) as the most critical choke point, PINR's physics engine reveals that California's many parallel lines easily absorb the load. Instead, the true physical bottlenecks hide in the power-exporting corridors of the Desert Southwest (Arizona and the Lower Colorado River) and the mountain seams connecting Montana, the Pacific Northwest, and Utah. items.summary: This paper investigates whether low-order packet-loss statistics suffice to assess survival-time risk under bursty packet losses, i.e., the probability that no update succeeds for a prescribed number of consecutive slots. Conventional models, such as the Gilbert model, characterize packet losses using the loss rate and mean burst length, but channels sharing these statistics may exhibit substantially different failure risks. We characterize the Markov channels one order above a given low-order fit that share its statistics and analyze their risks under acknowledgment-based scheduling with transmission budgets. We show that, with dense transmission attempts, risk is primarily governed by loss persistence beyond the modeled memory, and the worst-case channel need not be the most persistent one. Under limited budgets, retry spacing makes loss relapse probabilities important and can reverse the risk ordering of compatible channels. Numerical and measurement results show that low-order models can substantially underestimate the risk, highlighting the need for scheduling-dependent channel statistics.

items.summary: Scientific experiments are increasingly selected, executed and interpreted by learned systems that act through physical interfaces. Robot learning builds physical competence, whereas AI for science chooses which experiment to run, each reporting different endpoints. This review treats their interface as one problem, embodied AI for science, where the experiment itself is partially observed: specimen state, apparatus state and measurement processes are latent, actions are costly and irreversible, and missingness depends on execution and outcome. We organize the literature by three closures operating at distinct levels: operational closure (the experiment realized is the one intended), epistemic closure (the result updates beliefs or selects subsequent experiments) and evidential closure (the record supports a claim). We analyze workflows through a record-linked evidence cycle - Record, Diagnose, Calibrate, Confirm - as analytic functions with feedback. A taxonomy crosses these closures with six delegated decisions and five embodiment classes. Our formulation separates commanded, realized and observed conditions and models diagnosis with explicit resource, risk and sample-change costs. We compare experiment-selection methods by terminal decision, review perception, protocol compilation, visuomotor policies, world models, recovery and transfer by evidence emission requirements, and compare chemistry, materials, biology, microscopy and field workflows by what their records establish. An appendix provides an evidence map of 28 workflows (26 physical, two software-boundary), characterizing validation pathways and claim confirmation requirements. We propose evaluation that separates actions, valid experiments, campaigns and confirmed claims, framing open challenges as controlled comparisons with measurable failure conditions.

Arts 4. Natural Sciences 5. Social Sciences 6. Environmental and Technical Sciences 7. The framework distinguishes between unverified allegations, documented concerns, and substantiated findings. Bibliometric anomalies, retractions, or incomplete verification procedures must not automatically be interpreted as proof of individual research misconduct. The workbook also incorporates guidance for nominators regarding documentary evidence and the distinction between achievements that are not documented, criteria that have not yet been assessed, and verified absence of specific achievements. The assessment framework is intended to facilitate structured scholarly judgment rather than replace it. Its numerical weights and classification thresholds are illustrative methodological parameters and have not undergone independent empirical validation. Scope and limitations The instrument is proposed for academic discussion, methodological evaluation, pilot testing, and potential institutional adaptation. It is not an autonomous research misconduct detection system or a validated psychometric instrument. The workbook does not independently retrieve or verify bibliometric information. It brings together the foundational development of the model, revised property definitions and their algebraic consequences, corrected crown-network records, ecological reanalyses, editable network drawings, and software for reconstructing and analyzing existing or newly constructed WCHNs. The deposit is an independent scientific resource, not tied to a particular journal or manuscript. HISTORICAL FOUNDATION Four publications document the model's development: (1) Souza et al. (2011), the original network analysis of Cerrado crowns ( https://doi.org/10.1007/s11258-010-9797-7 ); (2) Prado et al. (2020), formalization of decomposition, topology, and four initial properties ( https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jtbi.2020.110318 ); (3) Prado and Trovão (2023), expansion to eight properties and Caatinga–Cerrado comparisons ( https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2023.110345 ); and (4) Prado (2024), stochastic node-addition networks and size-matched comparisons ( https://doi.org/10.1007/s40626-024-00340-5 ). These references allow users to trace the original definitions and later revisions. MATHEMATICAL AND EMPIRICAL CONTENT The author-prepared document “Algebraic relationships and mathematical properties of the Woody Crown Hydraulic Network” explains the revised symmetry (SYM), complexity (COM), and vulnerability (VUL) definitions, algebraic dependencies, network-size effects, and reproducibility checks. In particular, revised VUL is exactly equal to normalized mean node depth in a rooted tree. The observed near-reciprocity between navigability (NAV) and VUL is a strong empirical association, not a second exact identity or independent hydraulic measurement. The deposit retains the original Cerrado and Caatinga source spreadsheets, recalculated property tables, comparisons, reduced principal component analyses (PCAs), and size-adjusted exploratory analyses. The previously deposited PCA outputs are preserved numerically; their interpretations should account for the revised mathematical meaning of VUL. The updated PCA technical note documents the analytical methods and limitations. CORRECTED CERRADO NETWORKS AND TOOLKIT A new workbook records corrections to 20 previously sampled Cerrado WCHNs (not additional independent observations). Six networks were reconstructed manually, including S. polyphyllum 1 as the manual feasibility pilot; fourteen were reconstructed semi-automatically, beginning with S. camporum 1 as the first test of the connector generator, followed by thirteen additional networks. In the semi-automatic workflow, the researcher marked the nodes, deterministic software proposed editable connectors and highlighted ambiguous nodes in red, and the researcher visually checked and corrected the complete graph against the original drawing beneath it. The WCHN toolkit v1.0.3 contains code, documentation, editable PowerPoint networks, intermediate files, tests, and a separate semi-automatic validation exercise using Miconia albicans 5, a network originally reconstructed manually. That exercise led to a verified terminal-connector decomposition correction without changing the network topology or any of its eight WCHN properties. The accompanying Practical Guide v1.0.3 provides step-by-step instructions for reconstructing, inspecting, validating, and analyzing WCHNs, including optional AI assistance under mandatory researcher supervision. REPRODUCIBILITY AND LIMITATIONS The accompanying README.md provides the complete file inventory, foundational references, directions for reusing the toolkit and statistical scripts, links among materials, and version history. These resources enable checking corrected topologies and calculations and exploring

Two results on complementary (mutually unbiased) measurements and the complementary quantum correlation (CQC) inequality of Schneeloch, Broadbent and Howell (2014), which proposed that the classical correlations in two complementary measurement tables never exceed the quantum mutual information. 1. Sharp qutrit discrimination. For every pair of complementary bases of a qutrit and every two orthogonal states, the triangular discrimination summed over the two bases is at most 8/3 (the trivial ceiling is 4), answering Qian, arXiv:2608.14806v2, Section 11(4). Every equality case is classified; for the computational and Fourier bases they are tied to the nine Hesse SIC rays. Consequences: choosing one of the two measurements at random recovers at most two thirds of the quantum Fisher information in a two-state estimation task, and Qian's two-ray qubit-qutrit family obeys CQC with margin at least 0.1005 nats. The proof is computer-assisted: an exact rational sum-of-squares certificate (scout_qutrit/exact_sos_certificate.json, 660,609 bytes, SHA-256 825bb8108096d38a44f63f1bc91964405d189ad57b5f568530b5d8e27d598c2f) checked by a standalone exact verifier; this deposit is the certificate's citable locator. 2. Every prescribed pair fails for a qubit and a qudit of dimension n ≥ 4. For every prescribed pair of complementary measurements on each side there is a separable state violating CQC, with a uniform certified margin below −9/20,000,000 nats (previously the every-pair statement was known only for n ≥ 164). A phase-averaging extension of the known shared-label mechanism covers every prescribed pair when both dimensions are at least three; an earlier, unchecked every-pair statement for equal dimensions by E. O'Connor is credited. Open: the full qubit-qutrit CQC question and the sharp constant in dimension 5 (numerics only). The margins are tiny and structural, not experimental. The archive contains the manuscript (PDF and LaTeX), the exact certificate and verifier, negative controls, an exact rational margin checker, numerical cross-checks, working proof notes, novelty audits, the bibliography with registry records, CI and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: computer-assisted exact rational arithmetic, not a formal proof; internal AI-assisted review only (not human peer review or independent reproduction). Creator: Anonymous. Major findings (Virgo SCDM N-body simulation, redshifts z = 10 to 0): Kinematic relations of any order are derived for incompressible, constant-divergence and irrotational flow, and validated by the simulation. On large scales, third-order velocity correlations can be related to the density correlation or the pairwise velocity. The p-th order velocity correlations follow a^((p+2)/2) for odd p and a^(p/2) for even p (a = scale factor). The fitted exponents for odd p are smaller than these predictions. The overdensity is proportional to the density correlation on the same scale, <delta> ∝ <delta delta'>; the velocity dispersion on a scale r is proportional to the overdensity on that scale. The effective viscosity of the adhesion model originates from velocity fluctuations; the negative viscosity is due to the inverse energy cascade. On small scales, a self-closed velocity evolution is obtained by splitting velocity into motion within haloes and motion of haloes. Vorticity, enstrophy and energy evolution follow from it. The mean pairwise velocity follows <Δu_L> = −H a r. The third moment follows <(Δu_L)^3> ∝ ε_u a r, with a constant energy-cascade rate ε_u ≈ −4.6×10⁻⁷ m²/s³. items.summary: Progress in robot learning, particularly physical multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), is currently challenged by a limited availability of accessible, standardized benchmarks. While simulation-based MARL has produced remarkable emergent behaviors, from coordinated team play to complex tool use, translating these advances to physical systems remains difficult. A key barrier is infrastructural: physical platforms are often prohibitively expensive, require specialized facilities, or lack open mechanisms and designs for reproducibility. We introduce KlaskTron, an open-source, low-cost (<\$2500 USD), desktop-scale robotic testbed for adversarial MARL based on the dynamic tabletop game KLASK. The platform features dual CoreXY gantries with high-torque brushless motors, enabling the high-speed, precise manipulation required for competitive play. Crucially, we provide a complete ecosystem: hardware designs (CAD, BOM), a GPU-native digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Lab for high-fidelity modeling and simulation, and a validated sim-to-real baseline using a learned neural actuator model. We demonstrate that this baseline enables zero-shot policy transfer, with trained agents exhibiting emergent adversarial behaviors. To ensure full reproducibility of our results, all project assets are released publicly: hardware CAD/BOM and assembly documentation at [https://idscethzurich.github.io/klask_hardware], inference software stack at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_software] and the simulation and MARL setup at [https://github.com/IDSCETHZurich/klask_rl].

items.summary: Learning-based approaches have increasingly been explored for SAT solving, with particular attention to improving branching decisions in conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) solvers. These approaches derive branching guidance either from static structural properties of SAT formulas or from dynamic signals obtained through solver feedback and execution traces. However, these forms of supervision provide limited evidence about state-dependent branching effects, while different outcome measures may favor different branching choices. To address these limitations, we propose SAT-ACT, an outcome-derived learning framework for CDCL branching. We design three complementary outcome comparison criteria to extract action preferences from independent branching action rollouts initiated at the same solver state. The criteria identify preferences supported by the outcomes and leave comparisons unresolved when the evidence is insufficient or conflicting, instead of forcing an ordering using a predefined scalar metric. A state-conditioned network learns branching priorities from the extracted preferences and uses them to guide CDCL search directly without online action rollouts. We further introduce non-dominated heuristic action supervision, which retains the solver-selected action as a training target only when it remains non-dominated under these preferences. Solver-level experiments show that SAT-ACT consistently reduces CDCL search costs on three SAT families and improves PAR-2 on the SAT Competition benchmarks.
items.title: SAT-ACT: Learning CDCL Branching from Outcome-Derived Action Preferences
